name: Ohkami (rt_nio and rt_tokio builds)
baseline: Drogon 1.9.13 (C++, trantor event loop; the-benchmarker cpp/drogon, cmake release build); also agoo-c 0.7 (C) in the same table
workload: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks minimal HTTP contract (GET /, GET /user/:id, POST /user on port 3000), total_requests_per_s at 64, 256 and 512 connections, each framework in its own container.
claimed_speedup: ohkami-nio: 244,774 / 230,703 / 220,816 req/s at 64 / 256 / 512 connections vs Drogon 177,005 / 178,341 / 171,358 (1.38x / 1.29x / 1.29x, derived from page data). ohkami-tokio: 233,990 / 219,199 / 216,396 (1.32x / 1.23x / 1.26x vs Drogon, derived). vs agoo-c (C) 143,753 / 214,704 / 200,748: 1.70x at 64, 1.07x at 256, 1.10x at 512 (derived). p99 latency at 64 connections 0.000465 s (ohkami-nio) vs Drogon 0.01131 s (unit assumed seconds).
compiler_and_flags: Cargo release profile (read for the nio build only): lto = true, codegen-units = 1, panic = abort; Rust 1.98 docker image; ohkami 0.24 with feature rt_nio (nio 0.1) or rt_tokio. Drogon: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=release, no LTO.
hardware: data.json hardware field (published 2026-10-06): cpu_name 'M1 Eight-Core Processor', cpus 16, memory 7,733,008 kB, Linux 7.2.7-200.fc44.x86_64 (Fedora). Per-run server_cpu_cores / server_cpu_saturation imply about 4 CPUs allotted to each server container (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Rust framework with selectable runtimes (tokio, nio, smol, glommio, monoio, compio); the numbers here are for the nio and tokio builds only. Declarative API, HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/3.
caveats: The Ohkami README states no benchmark numbers and no mechanism; it only points at its benches directory. The two builds in the suite differ by under 6%. Whether Ohkami wraps hyper or has its own HTTP stack was not established from the pages read. Suite-level weaknesses: one published snapshot (data.json updated 2026-10-06, no per-run date, no repeat spread); the README says a run is server-bound only above 75% CPU saturation, the suite median is 71%, but the 60 fastest rows all sit at 49-63% (Drogon 62-63%, the winners here 49-62%), so the ceiling for the fastest servers may be the load generator or the box rather than the server; the README says methodology changed in 2026 and data.json carries no tool field, so whether this snapshot is the zrk closed-loop keep-alive revision or an older oha new-connection-per-request revision is not stated in the file; the workload is three trivial routes (GET /, GET /user/:id, POST /user) with near-empty bodies. The C++ side is only Drogon 1.9.13 (cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=release, threads_num 0 = auto, no LTO), oatpp 1.3 and two C servers; the best C row agoo-c 0.7 beats several of the winners below at 256 and 512 connections. nginx, h2o and lithium are not rows in this suite. Same table, losers to Drogon at 256 connections: Crystal toro 166,910, Go fasthttp 166,243, C# aspnet-minimal-api 147,805 vs Drogon 178,341, so no Crystal, Go-stdlib-level or .NET win exists here. Rated B, not A, because of the saturation and snapshot caveats; build files, language versions and CPU model are all public, so a verifier may raise it.

name: kawipiko
baseline: NGINX (distribution package; configuration in the kawipiko examples/nginx folder), also darkhttpd
workload: Static 'Hello World!' file served from a CDB archive held in memory (kawipiko) or from tmpfs (NGINX), wrk over loopback with keep-alive, 512 to 16384 connections; plus a 250k-file OpenStreetMap tile set at 16384 connections.
claimed_speedup: 512 connections, 2 server threads: kawipiko 106,698.89 req/s vs NGINX 79,816.08 (1.34x, derived from page data); 2048 connections: 100,296.65 vs 78,211.46; 4096: 95,628.34 vs 75,970.82; 16384: 53,548.52 vs 43,909.67. Tile benchmark (i7 4770, 8 threads, 16384 connections): kawipiko 238,499.86 req/s vs NGINX 188,255.32 (1.27x, derived), with ~25% more requests/s, ~29% lower average latency and ~25% less CPU per request stated by the author.
compiler_and_flags: Go build of kawipiko (version and flags not stated); NGINX from distribution packages (version and build flags not stated); server run with --archive-inmem, --security-headers-disable and --timeout-disable.
hardware: Laptop with Intel Core i7 3667U (2 physical cores, 4 threads), 8 GiB RAM for the Hello World runs; desktop Intel Core i7 4770 (4 cores, 8 threads), 32 GiB for the tile run; wrk and server pinned to separate physical cores, tmpfs.
tradeoffs: Serves only a prebuilt CDB archive, so content changes need a rebuild; HTTP/2 is about 6 times slower than its HTTP/1 path (Go net/http), where the author says NGINX is much better; kawipiko used about 1 GiB RAM in the tile run while NGINX used the least; AGPL licence.
caveats: First-party; the per-connection rows are marked 'Last updated in August 2018' and the summary 'December 2021', measured on 2013-era CPUs (i7 3667U, i7 4770), the author says the current version is at least 10% more efficient. NGINX is a distro package with an author-tuned config; timeouts and security headers are disabled in the kawipiko run (author says timeouts cost 10-15%). Socket errors and timeouts appear in the 2048 and 16384 connection rows for both servers. The author states the real advantage over NGINX is deployment simplicity, not raw speed, and calls the result 'at least on-par'.
found_via: WebSearch 'static file web server written in Rust OR Zig OR Go "faster than nginx" benchmark wrk requests/sec README comparison h2o lwan' (github.com, gitlab.com, codeberg.org filter)
why_faster: Content pre-indexed in a CDB archive held in memory with a compact lookup (no per-request file system calls), on Go fasthttp; the README says the advantage grows for many small files accessed in random patterns.
